# Detecting and controlling microbes

> *Two practical problems run through clinical microbiology: finding out in the laboratory which
> microbe is present, and removing unwanted microbes from instruments, surfaces and hands.*

## What each method reads {#sec-det-reads}

Each laboratory method detects one property of the organism, or of the host's response to it, and
that property sets what a result can and cannot show.

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/method-sorter.yml"></div>

## Seeing: stains and microscopy {#sec-det-microscopy}

Microscopy is fast, cheap and widely available, and it shows structure. The Gram stain, from [*How
bacteria are built and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-envelope), distinguishes the
two main envelope designs within minutes, and the acid-fast stain detects the waxy wall of
mycobacteria, which the Gram stain misses.

A stain gives a category, not a species: purple cocci in chains could be one of several organisms. It
also needs a large number of organisms in the sample, so a negative smear does not exclude infection.
Organisms with no wall, or too thin to resolve, give nothing useful.

## Growing: culture {#sec-det-culture}

Culture depends on growth, and its main advantage over every other method is that it yields a living
isolate, which can then be identified, tested against drugs, and compared with isolates from other
patients during an outbreak investigation. Media are chosen for what they allow to grow or what they
reveal.

| Type of medium | What it does | Example of use |
|---|---|---|
| Non-selective | Supports a wide range of organisms | A general plate for a sample from a normally sterile site |
| Enriched | Adds nutrients for **fastidious** organisms, which cannot make them | **Chocolate agar**, made with heated blood, which supplies factors released from lysed red cells |
| Selective | Contains agents that suppress unwanted organisms | Isolating one pathogen from a sample full of resident microbiota |
| Differential | Makes colonies look different according to a metabolic property | Blood agar, on which haemolysis distinguishes streptococci |

Culture conditions decide what a laboratory can find. In each of the following situations, a
negative culture does not mean that the sample contained nothing:

- An anaerobe will not grow on a plate kept in air, as in the lab case in [*How bacteria are built
  and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-case).
- A slow-growing organism is missed if plates are discarded too early, as in the *Helicobacter* case
  in [*The microbial world*](microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-case).
- An **obligate intracellular** organism, one that can grow only inside living host cells, such as
  *Chlamydia*, will not grow on agar at all.

Culture is also slow. Many bacteria need overnight incubation, and mycobacteria can take weeks, which
is the main reason molecular methods have become central.

## Detecting molecules {#sec-det-molecular}

**Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs)**, of which the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is the
best-known example, copy a target sequence many times until it can be detected. They are fast and
highly sensitive, and they can detect organisms that cannot be cultured. Their limits follow from what
they detect:

- They detect sequence, not viability. Dead organisms, or nucleic acid remaining after an infection has
  resolved, can give a positive result, so a positive test does not always mean active infection.
- They detect only their target. A test designed for one organism will not report another, whereas
  culture can grow an organism nobody was looking for.
- Their sensitivity makes contamination a real risk, which is why laboratories separate the work done
  before and after amplification.

Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionisation time-of-flight (**MALDI-TOF**) mass spectrometry identifies
a colony from its protein profile, matched against a database, within minutes once the organism has
grown. It has largely replaced long series of biochemical tests. **Whole-genome sequencing** determines
the entire genome, at a resolution that can show whether isolates from two patients belong to the same
strain, and it is now standard in outbreak investigation.

## Detecting the host's response: serology {#sec-det-serology}

**Serology** detects the patient's antibodies, so it is evidence about the host's history rather than
about the organism's presence now. IgM appears early and then falls; IgG appears later and persists,
sometimes for life. A fourfold or greater rise in antibody titre between **paired sera**, an acute-phase
sample and a convalescent sample taken two to four weeks later, indicates recent infection.

The usual pitfall follows directly: a single positive IgG result may reflect an infection years ago, or
vaccination. Serology is most useful for organisms that are hard to culture, for infections diagnosed
after the organism has gone, and for assessing immunity.

## Testing drug susceptibility {#sec-det-mic}

Once an organism has been grown, its susceptibility to drugs can be measured. The standard quantity is
the **minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC)**, the lowest concentration of a drug that prevents
visible growth.

<div data-island="mic-reader" data-src="/diagrams/mic-reader.yml"></div>

The laboratory converts the MIC into a category (susceptible, susceptible at increased exposure, or
resistant) using a **breakpoint**, the concentration agreed to separate infections likely to respond to
treatment from those that are not. Breakpoints are set by the European Committee on Antimicrobial
Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) and the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI), and are
revised as evidence accumulates, so they are looked up rather than memorised.

A report of "susceptible" describes the organism in a tube, not the patient: the drug still has to
reach the site of infection at an adequate concentration. Samples for culture should also be taken
before treatment starts, because even one dose of an antimicrobial can stop the organism growing in
the laboratory.

## Controlling microbes {#sec-det-control}

**Sterilisation**, **disinfection** and **antisepsis** mean different things:

- Sterilisation kills or removes all microbial life, including bacterial spores.
- Disinfection removes most organisms from an inanimate object, but does not reliably kill spores.
- Antisepsis applies the same idea to living tissue, as in skin preparation before a procedure.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-sterilisation-disinfection.yml"></div>

Organisms differ in what they survive:

- Bacterial spores survive boiling and alcohol, so instruments that enter sterile tissue are
  autoclaved.
- The lipid envelope of enveloped viruses is fragile, so alcohol and detergents inactivate these
  viruses readily.
- Non-enveloped viruses, such as the enteroviruses that cause hand, foot and mouth disease, are more
  resistant.
- Prions are not reliably inactivated by routine autoclaving and need specific, extended protocols.

From these differences we can predict when soap and water replace alcohol hand rub: when spores or
non-enveloped viruses are a concern, because washing removes physically what alcohol does not kill.

## Preventing infection {#sec-det-prevent}

Prevention acts on the links of the chain of infection in [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-chain).

**Vaccination** makes a host immune without causing disease. Vaccines differ in what they contain:

- inactivated organisms;
- live attenuated organisms;
- purified components, such as proteins or capsular polysaccharides;
- **toxoids** (inactivated protein toxins);
- nucleic acid encoding an antigen.

Capsular polysaccharides alone produce a poor response in young children, so they are linked to a
protein in a **conjugate vaccine**, which greatly improved protection against encapsulated bacteria.
Vaccines that reduce carriage or transmission also protect unvaccinated people, the herd immunity
effect; tetanus toxoid does not, because tetanus does not pass between people.

Antimicrobial stewardship (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-resistance)) limits selection for resistance by keeping
antimicrobial use to what is needed.
